prompt: Why is a five-year-old blog post a riskier source than the official docs for a library's current behavior?
choices: Blog posts are always technically wrong
The official docs update when the software changes; the blog post never does, so it may not match the current version
Blog posts don't include code examples
Search engines rank official docs lower than blog posts

prompt: You forgot the exact arguments `str.split()` accepts in Python. What's the most efficient first move?
choices: Search the web for a tutorial blog post about string splitting
Ask an AI assistant to write a splitting function from scratch
Go directly to the Python reference docs for str.split and scan for the signature
Read a full guide/tutorial on Python strings from the beginning

prompt: Before searching the web for how to use an unfamiliar flag on a CLI tool already installed on your machine, what should you try first?
choices: Searching Stack Overflow for the tool's name
Asking an AI assistant with no other context
Running the tool's --help or checking its man page
Reading the tool's GitHub issues for similar questions

prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the four parts of a good bug report?
choices: The exact error text, copied verbatim
A minimal reproduction of the problem
A guess at which library is secretly at fault, stated as fact
What you already tried

prompt: A teammate pastes their entire 400-line file into an AI assistant with the message 'this is broken, fix it.' What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The assistant will always find and fix the exact bug immediately
The assistant may guess wrong about what 'broken' means or which lines matter, producing a plausible but off-target fix
The assistant will refuse to respond to files over 100 lines
Pasting more code always produces a more accurate fix than pasting less

prompt: You're testing whether your 'minimal reproduction' of a bug is actually minimal. What should you do?
choices: Trust it once it's under 20 lines
Delete lines one at a time and confirm the bug still happens after each deletion; if it still reproduces after a deletion, it wasn't minimal yet
Add more context so the reader has full background, even if unrelated to the bug
Rewrite the whole reproduction from memory without testing it again

prompt: What is the key similarity between writing a good Stack-Overflow-style bug report and writing a good debugging prompt to an AI assistant?
choices: Both require you to withhold the exact error message so the reader has to ask follow-up questions
Both are unnecessary if you paste the entire codebase
Both benefit from the same underlying discipline: isolate the problem, quote the exact error, state expected vs. actual, and say what's already been ruled out
AI assistants require far less detail than human readers because they can infer missing context
